chapters.n: The book opens by naming its author as “the Preacher,” a son of David who ruled in Jerusalem. Tradition identifies him with Solomon, the king famous for his wisdom, though many scholars think a later writer used Solomon’s voice.

f.g: Hebrew Qoheleth — one who gathers an assembly and speaks to it; the Greek title Ecclesiastes means the same.

chapters.n: This is the book’s theme sentence. “Vanity of vanities” is a Hebrew way of saying “the most fleeting thing of all.” Life lived only for earthly things vanishes like a breath.

f.g: Hebrew hebel — breath, vapor, mist; something brief, empty, or impossible to grasp, not pride.

chapters.n: The Preacher asks the question the whole book explores: what lasting gain do people get from all their hard work? “Under the sun” means life viewed from a purely earthly point of view.

f.g: Hebrew yitron — what is left over; lasting gain or advantage.
A phrase used about 29 times in the book: life as seen from the earth alone.

chapters.n: People come and go, but the earth stays. Compared with the steady earth, a single human life seems short and small.
The sun rises, sets, and hurries back to rise again. The picture is of endless, tiring repetition that never seems to arrive anywhere new.

f.g: Literally “pants” — like a runner gasping as he hurries back to the starting line.

chapters.n: The wind circles south and north and round again. Like the sun, it is busy but keeps returning to the same paths.

f.g: Circular courses; the wind’s regular rounds.

chapters.n: Rivers keep pouring into the sea, yet the sea never fills up. Nature illustrates effort that never reaches completion.
Everything is wearisome beyond words. Human desire is never satisfied: our eyes always want to see more and our ears to hear more.

f.g: Or “full of weariness” — everything is tiresome.

chapters.n: History repeats itself. What happened before will happen again, and nothing is truly new in human experience when seen only from below.

f.w: no new thing under the sun
f.g: Contrast God’s promise of a “new thing” and a new heaven and earth (Isaiah 43:19; Revelation 21:5).

chapters.n: When people think they have found something new, it usually turns out to have existed long before. We simply don’t remember the past well.

f.g: In ages past.

chapters.n: Past generations are forgotten, and future ones will be forgotten too. The Preacher feels how quickly human memory fades.
The Preacher introduces himself personally as a king over Israel. What follows is his own report of his search for meaning.
He set out to study everything people do. He calls this search for understanding a heavy task God has given humanity to keep us busy and thinking.

f.g: A painful, burdensome task.
Occupied or kept busy.

chapters.n: After seeing all human activity, he concludes it is fleeting and like trying to catch the wind.

f.g: Better “striving after wind” or “chasing the wind” — effort that grasps nothing.

chapters.n: Some problems simply can’t be fixed by human effort, and what is missing can’t be counted as if it were there. Wisdom has limits.

f.g: Lacking or missing.

chapters.n: Talking to himself, the Preacher admits he gained more wisdom than anyone before him in Jerusalem. He had every advantage for this search.

f.g: Thought things through privately; talked with himself.

chapters.n: He studied both wisdom and its opposites — madness and foolishness — to understand life fully. Even that study felt like chasing wind.
The more he understood, the more he saw life’s pain and injustice. Knowledge without God’s larger view can bring sorrow rather than peace.

f.g: Wisdom opens one’s eyes to suffering; the book later points to fearing God as the answer (Ecclesiastes 12:13).

chapters.n: The Preacher decides to test whether pleasure can satisfy. He tells his heart to enjoy itself, but finds pleasure just as fleeting.

f.g: An old phrase meaning “Come now” or “Let’s try.”
Test.

chapters.n: Laughter and fun, he concludes, are a kind of madness when chased for their own sake. They accomplish nothing lasting.

f.g: What does it achieve?

chapters.n: He experiments with wine and even folly, while trying to keep his mind wise, to discover what is truly good for people in their short lives.

f.g: Still guiding himself by wisdom during the experiment.

chapters.n: He turns to great building projects — houses and vineyards. Solomon was known for vast construction, including the temple and his palace.
He plants gardens and orchards full of every kind of fruit tree, creating a kind of paradise for himself.

f.g: Hebrew pardes, a Persian loanword for an enclosed park — the source of our word “paradise.”

chapters.n: He builds reservoirs to irrigate forests of young trees. In a dry land, this was a sign of great wealth and engineering.

f.g: Large reservoirs; ancient pools south of Bethlehem are traditionally called “Solomon’s Pools.”

chapters.n: He gathers many servants and huge herds, more than anyone before him in Jerusalem. He lacked nothing in possessions.

f.g: Servants whose families had served the household for generations.
Large and small livestock — herds and flocks.

chapters.n: He piles up silver, gold, royal treasures, singers, and every kind of entertainment. Every pleasure money could buy was his.

f.g: Special or prized treasure, like tribute from other kings.

chapters.n: He became greater than anyone before him, yet he kept his wisdom. He wasn’t lost in pleasure; he was watching it carefully.

f.g: He stayed clear-headed throughout the experiment.

chapters.n: He denied himself nothing he wanted, and he did enjoy his work. That enjoyment was the only reward the work gave him.

f.g: Share or allotted reward.

chapters.n: Looking back at all he built and enjoyed, he found it empty — like chasing the wind. Nothing gave lasting gain.
He turns to compare wisdom with foolishness. Any king after him can only repeat what he has already tried, so his findings stand.

f.g: His successor — no one will have more resources to test life than he did.

chapters.n: Wisdom really is better than folly — as much better as light is than darkness. The Preacher doesn’t deny wisdom’s value.
The wise person can see where he is going, while the fool stumbles in the dark. Yet the same fate — death — comes to both.

f.g: He sees clearly and watches his steps.
One outcome or fate: death.

chapters.n: If he will die like the fool anyway, he wonders what good his extra wisdom did him. This too seems empty.
Both wise and foolish are soon forgotten after they die. From an earthly view, death seems to erase every difference.
Seeing this, he felt disgust for life itself, because all earthly work seemed fleeting. He honestly describes a season of despair.
He hated his own achievements because he would have to leave them all to someone else when he died.

f.w: leave it unto the man that shall be after me

chapters.n: His heir might be wise or a fool, yet would control everything he built. History shows Solomon’s son Rehoboam lost most of the kingdom through poor judgment.
He let himself sink into despair about all his hard work.

f.g: To give up hope; literally to make his heart lose heart.

chapters.n: Someone may work with skill and fairness, only to hand it all to a person who did nothing to earn it. The Preacher calls this a real wrong.

f.g: Fairness, uprightness.

chapters.n: So what does a person really get out of all the toil and anxiety of life?
Work brings sorrow by day and sleepless worry by night. Even rest escapes the anxious worker.

f.g: Toil, hard labor.

chapters.n: Here is a key insight: the simple ability to enjoy food, drink, and one’s work is a gift from God. Joy comes from His hand, not from striving.
No one has tested enjoyment more than the Preacher, so he speaks from experience: real enjoyment depends on God.

f.g: Hurry after enjoyment.

chapters.n: God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy to those who please Him, while the sinner gathers wealth that ends up with the righteous. Even so, from below life still feels fleeting.

f.w: giveth to a man that is good

chapters.n: This famous poem begins with its main idea: everything in life has its proper season. God has set a time for each human experience.

f.g: An appointed time.
Matter, activity, or desire.

chapters.n: Life moves between opposites — birth and death, planting and harvesting. The poem pairs fourteen opposites, a number suggesting completeness (twice seven).

f.g: Uproot or harvest.

chapters.n: There are times for ending and times for healing, for tearing down and for building. Even painful seasons have their place in God’s order.
Grief and joy each have their time. Mourning and dancing are both part of a full human life.
Scattering and gathering stones may refer to clearing or building on farmland, and embracing and refraining to times of closeness and distance.

f.g: Possibly clearing a field of rocks, or spoiling an enemy’s field; the exact meaning is uncertain.

chapters.n: There are times to seek and gain, and times to let things go. Wisdom knows when to hold on and when to release.

f.g: Seek or gain.

chapters.n: Tearing clothing was a sign of mourning, and sewing it back a sign that grief had passed. There is also wisdom in knowing when to stay quiet and when to speak.

f.g: Tear — as people tore their clothes in grief.

chapters.n: Even love and hatred, war and peace, have their seasons in a fallen world. The poem ends on peace, a hopeful note.
After the poem, the Preacher returns to his question: if every season is set by God, what does a worker’s effort really add?
He has seen the burden of work God has given people to keep them occupied.
God makes everything beautiful in its proper time and has placed a longing for eternity in human hearts. Yet we can’t fully understand His work from start to finish.

f.g: Hebrew ‘olam — often “eternity”; God has put a sense of the eternal in people’s hearts.

chapters.n: The best thing people can do is to be glad and to do good while they live.
Being able to eat, drink, and find joy in one’s work is itself a gift from God.
What God does is permanent and complete; nothing can be added or removed. This is meant to fill people with reverent awe.

f.g: Reverence and awe toward God, not mere terror.

chapters.n: The patterns of the past recur, and God “seeks again” what has passed — He holds the past accountable and nothing slips from His notice.

f.g: Literally “seeks what has been driven away” — God calls the past back for judgment.

chapters.n: The Preacher saw corruption even in courts of justice: where righteousness should rule, wickedness had taken its place.

f.g: The law court.

chapters.n: Yet he trusts that God will judge both the righteous and the wicked, because God has a set time for every deed.
God allows these trials to test people and help them see that, left to themselves, they are as mortal as animals. It is a lesson in humility.

f.g: Test or sift; make plain what they are.

chapters.n: From an earthly view, humans and animals share the same fate: both breathe, and both die. In this sense people have no advantage.

f.g: Hebrew ruach — breath, wind, or spirit.
Advantage or superiority.

chapters.n: Both bodies return to the dust they came from, just as God told Adam.
He asks who can know for sure whether a human spirit goes up and an animal’s goes down. Later he affirms the spirit returns to God (12:7).

f.w: the spirit of man that goeth upward

chapters.n: So, he concludes, the best thing is to find joy in one’s own work, since no one can see what comes after this life from an earthly view.

f.g: Allotted share in life.

chapters.n: The Preacher looks at oppression and sees the tears of victims with no one to comfort them, while their oppressors hold all the power. The repeated phrase stresses their loneliness.
Overwhelmed by such suffering, he says the dead seem better off than the living who must endure it.
Better still, he says, is the one never born, who never had to see the evil done on earth. This is honest lament, not a teaching that life lacks worth.
Much hard work and success is driven by envy and rivalry with one’s neighbor. Competition of that kind is just chasing the wind.

f.g: Skillful or successful work.

chapters.n: On the other hand, the lazy fool who folds his hands ends up destroying himself. Idleness is no answer either.

f.g: Ruins himself; starves by his own laziness.

chapters.n: The balanced path: one handful with peace is better than two handfuls gained through stress and striving.

f.g: Rest, calm contentment.

chapters.n: He turns to another example of life’s emptiness.
A man with no family works endlessly and is never satisfied with his wealth. He never stops to ask who he is working for or why he denies himself joy.

f.g: Deprive myself of enjoyment.
Unhappy business; a heavy burden.

chapters.n: Companionship makes work more rewarding. Two people working together accomplish more than one alone.
If one falls, the other can help him up. The person who has no one is in real danger when trouble comes.

f.w: woe to him that is alone

chapters.n: On cold desert nights, travelers slept close for warmth. Companions protect and comfort one another.
Two can defend against an attacker better than one, and a rope of three strands is very hard to break. Many readers see in this a picture of marriage with God as the third strand.

f.g: Overpower him.
A rope braided from three strands — far stronger than one or two.

chapters.n: A poor young person who is wise is better than an old king who will no longer listen to advice. Position means nothing without teachableness.

f.g: Warned or counseled.

chapters.n: Such a youth may rise from prison to the throne, while one born royal may end up poor. Fortunes can reverse completely.

f.w: out of prison he cometh to reign
f.g: Recalls Joseph rising from prison to rule in Egypt (Genesis 41:14, 41).

chapters.n: He watches crowds rally behind the young successor who replaces the old king.

f.g: The youth who succeeds the king.

chapters.n: Yet the crowds are endless, and the next generation will forget even the popular new leader. Public favor is fleeting too.
Walk carefully when you go to worship. It is better to come ready to listen and obey than to offer careless sacrifices like fools who don’t realize they are doing wrong.

f.g: Watch your step — approach God with care and reverence.

chapters.n: Don’t rush into hasty promises or wordy prayers before God. He is in heaven and we are on earth, so let reverence keep our words few and sincere.
Just as too much busyness produces restless dreams, too many words reveal a fool. Chatter is not the same as devotion.

f.g: Many cares or much activity.

chapters.n: When you make a promise to God, keep it quickly. God takes no pleasure in people who make vows lightly and then forget them.
It is better not to make a vow at all than to make one and break it. This applies naturally to the covenants we make with God today.
Don’t let your mouth lead you into sin, and don’t excuse a broken vow to the priest by calling it a mistake. Why provoke God to undo the work of your hands?

f.g: Hebrew mal’ak — messenger; likely the temple priest who received vows (compare Malachi 2:7).

chapters.n: Many dreams and many words are empty. The answer is simple: revere God.

f.g: Various, many kinds of.

chapters.n: Don’t be shocked when officials oppress the poor and twist justice. Each official is watched by a higher one — and above all of them is God.

f.g: Don’t be astonished.
Each official guards his turf above another; ultimately God sees all.

chapters.n: The land’s produce benefits everyone; even a king depends on the fields. Society, high and low, rests on honest farming.

f.w: the king himself is served by the field
f.g: The Hebrew is difficult; it may mean a king who cares for the farmland benefits the land.

chapters.n: Whoever loves money will never have enough, and whoever loves wealth is never satisfied with more. Greed has no finish line.
As wealth grows, so do the people who consume it. The owner often gets little more than the pleasure of looking at it.

f.g: Except for watching them.

chapters.n: A worker sleeps well whether he eats much or little, but the rich man’s worries keep him awake at night.

f.g: Allow him.

chapters.n: The Preacher has seen a painful evil: wealth hoarded by its owner that ends up harming him.

f.g: A grievous wrong or sickening misfortune.

chapters.n: Then the riches are lost in a bad venture, and when he has a son there is nothing left to give him.

f.g: An unlucky business deal or misfortune.

chapters.n: We are born with nothing and we die with nothing. No earthly possession can be carried out of this life.
It is tragic that a person leaves exactly as he came. What did he gain by working for the wind?
Such a person lives his days in gloom, filled with frustration, sickness, and anger.

f.g: Lives joylessly and anxiously.

chapters.n: The Preacher’s positive counsel: it is good and fitting to enjoy food, drink, and work during the life God gives. That enjoyment is our God-given share.

f.g: Fitting, proper, beautiful.

chapters.n: When God gives someone wealth and also the ability to enjoy it with gratitude, that combination is a true gift from God.
Such a person won’t brood over life’s brevity, because God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart.

f.g: God keeps him busy (or answers him) with gladness.

chapters.n: The Preacher describes another sad situation he has seen often among people.
A man may have riches, wealth, and honor — everything he wants — yet be unable to enjoy any of it, while a stranger ends up enjoying it instead. That is a kind of sickness.

f.g: Lacks nothing.
A grievous affliction.

chapters.n: Even a man with a hundred children and a very long life, if he never finds satisfaction and isn’t honored at death, is worse off than a stillborn child.

f.g: In Israel, lacking a proper burial was a great disgrace (Jeremiah 22:18-19).
A miscarried or stillborn child.

chapters.n: The stillborn child comes into the world in futility, leaves in darkness, and its name is never known.

f.g: Arrives for nothing — its life passes as a breath.

chapters.n: It never saw the sun or knew anything, yet it has more rest than the restless, unsatisfied man.
Even living two thousand years would not help if a person never enjoyed any good. Everyone ends in the same grave.

f.g: Counted twice — two thousand years.

chapters.n: People work hard to feed themselves, yet their hunger always returns. Earthly appetite can never be permanently filled.
What advantage does the wise person have over the fool, or the poor person who knows how to conduct himself well? From below, it’s hard to say.

f.g: Behave wisely in society.

chapters.n: Enjoying what is in front of you is better than endlessly craving what you don’t have. Restless desire is chasing the wind.

f.g: The roaming of the appetite; endless craving.

chapters.n: Everything that exists has already been named and defined, and humanity is known for what it is: mortal. No one can argue with God, who is stronger.

f.w: it is known that it is man
f.g: Possibly a play on Adam (“man”) from adamah (“ground”) — humans are made of earth.

f.w: contend with him that is mightier

chapters.n: The more words people use arguing with God or life, the more empty it becomes. Talking doesn’t make anyone better off.

f.g: Or “many words.”

chapters.n: Who knows what is truly good for a person in this brief, shadow-like life? And who can tell what will happen after he is gone? These questions prepare for the book’s conclusion.
A good reputation is worth more than expensive perfume. And the day of death, when a life is complete, can be better than the day of birth, when everything is still uncertain.

f.g: A wordplay in Hebrew: “name” (shem) and “ointment” (shemen).

chapters.n: A funeral teaches more than a party, because it reminds us that everyone will die. The living should take that lesson to heart.

f.g: Take it seriously; reflect on it.

chapters.n: Sorrow can do more good than laughter, because sadness can soften and improve the heart.
The wise think seriously about death and life’s meaning, while fools think only about fun.
It is better to accept correction from a wise person than to listen to the songs and flattery of fools.
A fool’s laughter is like thorns crackling under a cooking pot — loud, quick, and soon gone, producing little heat.

f.w: crackling of thorns under a pot
f.g: Another Hebrew wordplay: “thorns” (sirim) under a “pot” (sir).

chapters.n: Being oppressed can drive even a wise person to act foolishly, and bribes corrupt the heart.
The end of a matter is better than its beginning, and patience is better than pride. Waiting to see how things turn out is wise.
Don’t be quick to get angry; anger settles in the heart of fools.

f.w: hasty in thy spirit to be angry

chapters.n: Don’t ask why the “good old days” were better than today. That question isn’t wise; every age has its blessings and trials.
Wisdom is as valuable as an inheritance, and it benefits everyone who lives under the sun.

f.g: The living.

chapters.n: Both wisdom and money offer protection, but wisdom has the greater advantage: it preserves life itself.

f.g: Literally “shade” or “shelter.”

chapters.n: Think about how God works: no one can straighten what He has allowed to be bent. Some trials must simply be accepted.
When times are good, be glad; when times are hard, stop and reflect. God allows both so people cannot predict the future and must trust Him.

f.g: Reflect, think it over.

chapters.n: In his life he has seen good people die young and wicked people live long. Life does not always seem fair in the short run.

f.g: My fleeting life.

chapters.n: Don’t be self-righteous or a know-it-all. Pride in one’s own goodness or wisdom can ruin a person.

f.g: Likely means self-righteous or showily pious, not truly good.
Ruin or isolate yourself.

chapters.n: Nor should you plunge into wickedness or foolishness, which can bring an early death.
Hold on to both warnings. The person who reverences God will avoid both extremes.

f.g: Escape all these dangers.

chapters.n: Wisdom gives a person more strength than ten powerful rulers in a city.
Everyone sins; there is no one on earth who always does good. This is why all people need God’s mercy.

f.w: there is not a just man

chapters.n: Don’t pay attention to every word people say, or you may overhear even your servant criticizing you.
After all, you know you have criticized others yourself. Be forgiving of what others say.
He tested all this with wisdom and resolved to be truly wise, but full wisdom stayed beyond his reach.

f.g: Tested.

chapters.n: The deepest truths are far off and profoundly deep — who can discover them? Only God fully understands.
He set himself to understand wisdom and the reasons behind things, and also the wickedness and madness of foolish living.

f.g: The sum or explanation of things.

chapters.n: He found something worse than death: the seductive woman of Proverbs whose love is a trap. Those who please God escape her; the sinner is caught.

f.g: Chains, fetters.

chapters.n: The Preacher says he weighed things one by one, trying to reach a final total.

f.g: The sum; the conclusion.

chapters.n: He kept searching but found few truly upright people — one in a thousand men, and among the women he dealt with, none. Many read this as reflecting his own life (compare 1 Kings 11:3), not a judgment on all women.

f.g: Solomon had a thousand wives and concubines (1 Kings 11:3), which may color this bitter remark.

chapters.n: His firm conclusion: God made people upright, but they have devised many schemes of their own. The problem lies in human choices, not in God’s creation.

f.g: Schemes or devices.

chapters.n: Who is truly wise and can explain the meaning of things? Wisdom lights up a person’s face and softens a harsh or stern expression.

f.g: Hardness or sternness of expression.

chapters.n: The Preacher advises obeying the king, partly because of the sacred oath of loyalty taken before God.

f.g: An oath sworn in God’s name, perhaps an oath of allegiance to the king.

chapters.n: Don’t storm out of the king’s presence or join a bad cause, since a king can do whatever he wants.

f.w: stand not in an evil thing
f.g: Don’t persist in a wrong course or plot.

chapters.n: A king’s word carries authority; no one can challenge him. Wise subjects respect that power.
Those who obey will stay out of trouble, and a wise heart knows the right time and right way to act.

f.g: The proper time and procedure.

chapters.n: There is a right time and way for everything, yet people suffer because they often don’t know them.
No one knows the future or can tell when things will happen.

f.w: knoweth not that which shall be

chapters.n: No one can hold back the breath of life or control the day of death. There’s no release from that battle, and wickedness won’t rescue those who practice it.

f.g: Hold on to the breath of life.
No one is excused from serving in death’s battle.

chapters.n: He has watched how people exercise power over others, sometimes to their own harm.
He saw wicked people buried with honor after coming and going from the holy place, and then praised in the city where they did evil. That too is empty.

f.g: Likely the temple.

chapters.n: Because punishment for evil isn’t carried out quickly, people grow bold in doing wrong. Delayed justice can encourage sin.
Even if a sinner does wrong a hundred times and lives long, the Preacher is sure that things will go well for those who reverence God.

f.w: it shall be well with them that fear God

chapters.n: But it will not go well for the wicked; his days will pass like a shadow because he refuses to revere God.

f.w: not be well with the wicked

chapters.n: Here is a puzzle: sometimes good people suffer what the wicked deserve, and the wicked enjoy what the righteous deserve. Earthly life doesn’t always reflect divine justice.

f.w: according to the work of the wicked

chapters.n: So the Preacher recommends enjoying life — eating, drinking, and being glad — as God’s gift that stays with us through our labor.

f.g: Praised joy and gladness.

chapters.n: When he devoted himself to understanding all that goes on in the world, he saw people so busy they barely sleep.

f.w: neither day nor night seeth sleep
f.g: An idiom for restless, sleepless effort.

chapters.n: Then he realized that no one can fully understand God’s work. Even the wisest who claim to know cannot discover it all.
After reflection he declares that the righteous and wise, and all their deeds, are in God’s hands. No one can tell from outward circumstances whether God favors them.
The same fate — death — comes to everyone: righteous and wicked, worshipers and non-worshipers, honest and dishonest alike.

f.g: One who swears oaths carelessly, compared to one who respects them.

chapters.n: It seems wrong that everyone shares one end, and that people’s hearts are full of evil and madness during life before they die.
As long as a person is alive there is hope. A living dog — a despised animal — is better off than a dead lion, the king of beasts.

f.w: a living dog is better than a dead lion
f.g: Dogs were scorned scavengers in Israel; lions symbolized power.

chapters.n: The living at least know they will die, but the dead know nothing more of this world and have no further earthly reward. Latter-day scripture teaches that the spirit lives on (Alma 40:11-14); the Preacher speaks of life “under the sun.”

f.w: the dead know not any thing

chapters.n: Their love, hatred, and envy are gone, and they no longer share in anything that happens on earth.
So go and enjoy your food and wine with a glad heart, for God approves of your living joyfully and gratefully.

f.g: God has already approved such joyful, grateful living.

chapters.n: Always wear clean, white clothes and fragrant oil — signs of festivity and gladness in the ancient world.

f.g: Scented oil worn on happy occasions.

chapters.n: Enjoy life with the wife you love throughout your brief life. Married love is one of God’s great gifts and your true portion.

f.w: Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest

chapters.n: Whatever you do, do it with all your strength, because opportunities to work and learn in mortal life end at death.

f.g: Planning or thought.
Hebrew Sheol — the world of the dead.

chapters.n: Success doesn’t always go to the fastest, strongest, wisest, or most skilled. Unforeseen events and timing affect everyone.

f.w: the race is not to the swift

f.g: Unexpected circumstances and occurrences.

chapters.n: No one knows when misfortune will strike. Like fish caught in a net or birds in a trap, people are often caught suddenly by hard times.

f.g: The time of his calamity or death.

chapters.n: He shares an example of wisdom that impressed him deeply.
A powerful king besieged a small city with few defenders, building great siege works against it.

f.g: Siege ramps or towers.

chapters.n: A poor but wise man in the city saved it by his wisdom — yet afterward no one remembered him.
Wisdom is better than strength, yet the poor man’s wisdom is despised and his advice ignored. People often value status over sound counsel.
The quiet words of the wise deserve more attention than the shouting of a ruler over fools.
Wisdom is better than weapons, but a single sinner can undo a great deal of good.
A few dead flies can make expensive perfume stink. In the same way, a little foolishness can ruin the reputation of someone known for wisdom.

f.g: Perfumer or maker of ointments.
Smell.

chapters.n: A wise heart leans toward what is right, while a fool’s heart leans the wrong way. The right hand symbolized strength and favor in the ancient world.
Even walking down the road, a fool shows his lack of sense and makes his foolishness obvious to everyone.

f.g: Literally “his heart is lacking” — he lacks sense.

chapters.n: If a ruler gets angry with you, don’t quit your post. Calm and gentleness can settle even great offenses.

f.g: Calmness soothes.

chapters.n: The Preacher notes a kind of mistake rulers make.
Fools get promoted to high positions while capable, wealthy people are given lowly places.

f.g: Here the noble or capable, in contrast to fools.

chapters.n: He has seen servants riding horses like nobles, and princes walking on foot like servants — a world turned upside down.
Every task carries risk: one who digs a pit may fall in, and one who breaks through a stone wall may be bitten by a snake hiding there. Plotting harm often backfires.

f.g: A stone wall, where snakes often hid.

chapters.n: Quarrying stones or splitting wood can injure the worker. Life calls for caution and skill.

f.g: Splits.

chapters.n: A dull axe takes more effort; sharpening it first is smarter. Wisdom helps people succeed with less wasted strength.

f.g: Sharpen.

chapters.n: If a snake bites before it is charmed, the snake charmer gains nothing. Skill is useless if not used at the right time.

f.g: Snake-charming.
Literally “master of the tongue” — the charmer.

chapters.n: A wise person’s words are kind and win favor, but a fool’s own talk destroys him.
A fool’s speech starts in foolishness and ends in destructive madness.

f.g: Harmful, wicked.

chapters.n: Fools talk on and on, though no one knows the future or what happens after them.
A fool’s work wears him out because he can’t even find his way to town. He lacks basic common sense.
Pity the nation whose king is immature and whose leaders feast in the morning instead of working.

f.g: Party when they should be judging and working.

chapters.n: Happy is the nation whose king is noble and whose leaders eat at the proper time, for strength rather than drunkenness.

f.g: At the proper time.

chapters.n: Through laziness the roof sags, and idle hands let the house leak. Neglect slowly ruins homes — and nations.

f.g: Leaks.

chapters.n: Feasts bring laughter and wine brings cheer, but money pays for everything. The verse may be a sly comment on careless leaders.

f.g: Money meets every demand — often read ironically.

chapters.n: Don’t curse the king even in your thoughts or the rich even in private, because word gets around in unexpected ways. The saying “a little bird told me” comes from this idea.

f.w: a bird of the air shall carry the voice
f.g: Secrets have a way of spreading.

chapters.n: Be generous and take wise risks, even when the return seems uncertain. Like grain shipped across the sea, kindness and investment often come back in time.

f.w: Cast thy bread upon the waters
f.g: Possibly sea trade or generous giving; both readings teach bold, faithful generosity.

chapters.n: Share with many people — seven, even eight — because you don’t know what hardships may come. Generosity builds a safety net of goodwill.

f.g: A Hebrew way of saying “many, and then some more.”

chapters.n: Some things just happen according to nature: full clouds pour rain, and a fallen tree stays where it lands. We can’t control everything.
If you wait for perfect weather, you’ll never plant or harvest. Too much caution leads to doing nothing.

f.g: Watches anxiously for perfect conditions.

chapters.n: Just as we don’t understand how life forms in the womb, we can’t understand all of God’s works. Trust Him and act anyway.

f.g: Hebrew ruach — wind, breath, or spirit; how life enters a baby.

f.w: bones do grow in the womb

chapters.n: Work diligently morning and evening, since you never know which effort will succeed — or whether both will.
Life is sweet; it is a joy to see the light of the sun. The Preacher affirms the goodness of being alive.
However long you live, enjoy every year, but remember that dark days will also come. Everything ahead is fleeting.

f.g: Old age, hardship, and finally death.

chapters.n: Young people should enjoy their youth and follow their heart’s good desires — while remembering that God will hold them accountable for their choices.

f.w: God will bring thee into judgment

chapters.n: So put away worry and avoid what harms your body, because youth passes quickly.

f.g: Youth is a fleeting breath — use it well.

f.w: put away evil from thy flesh

chapters.n: The book’s great appeal to the young: remember your Creator now, before the hard years of old age arrive when life feels joyless. Choosing God early shapes everything.

f.g: Troubled years of old age and decline.

chapters.n: Before life’s lights grow dim and troubles keep returning like clouds after rain. Many read verses 2–6 as a poetic picture of growing old.

f.w: the clouds return after the rain
f.g: Troubles that keep coming back, one after another.

chapters.n: In old age, the “keepers of the house” (hands and arms) shake, the “strong men” (legs) bend, the “grinders” (teeth) are few, and the “windows” (eyes) grow dim.

f.g: Likely the arms and hands.
Teeth.

f.w: those that look out of the windows
f.g: The eyes.

chapters.n: The “doors” (ears or lips) close, sounds grow faint, the elderly wake at the first birdsong, and singing voices fade.

f.w: rise up at the voice of the bird
f.g: Wake very early, as the elderly often do.
Songs or singing voices — or the voice and hearing.

chapters.n: The old fear heights and dangers on the road; hair turns white like almond blossoms; even a grasshopper feels heavy; and desire fades — until one goes to his eternal home amid mourners.

f.g: Almond blossoms are white — a picture of white hair.
Eternal home: the grave.

chapters.n: Before life’s thread snaps: a silver cord breaks, a golden lamp-bowl shatters, the water jar breaks at the spring, the well’s wheel falls apart. All are images of death.

f.g: Often understood as the cord of life that holds the lamp, or the bond between body and spirit.
A lamp bowl hanging from a cord; when it falls, the light goes out.

chapters.n: At death the body returns to dust and the spirit returns to God who gave it. Latter-day Saints see here the truth that our spirits came from God and return to Him.

f.w: the dust return to the earth
the spirit shall return unto God who gave it

chapters.n: The book ends where it began: life lived only “under the sun” is a passing breath. This frame prepares for the final conclusion.
A narrator now describes the Preacher: because he was wise, he kept teaching people, carefully studying and arranging many proverbs.
The Preacher looked for pleasing, fitting words, and what he wrote was honest and true.

f.g: Delightful or well-chosen words.

chapters.n: Wise sayings are like goads that prod oxen forward and like firmly driven nails that hold steady. They all come from one Shepherd — God.

f.g: Pointed sticks used to prod livestock.

chapters.n: Be warned, my son: there is no end to writing books, and endless study wears out the body. Learning is good, but it must lead somewhere.

f.g: Take warning.

chapters.n: The conclusion of everything: reverence God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole purpose of human life. Here the book’s search finds its answer.

f.w: Fear God, and keep his commandments

f.g: Literally “this is the whole of man” — what every person is for.

chapters.n: God will judge every deed, even secret ones, whether good or evil. Because judgment is real, life is not meaningless after all.
